Let no one be sluggish in devotion to her. Let no one omit her commemoration. For Anna is interpreted as “grace” or “gift.” A name fitting so great a parent, which we believe was not given to her at birth by chance, but was foreordained by God. For she is rightly interpreted as “grace,” since she was to bear the mother of grace. Rightly “grace,” through whose intercession the grace of God is obtained for the faithful. She is also interpreted as “one who gives,” or “gift,” because those whom she finds devout in her honor she makes rich with many gifts of grace. Rightly “gift,” through whom the remission of sins is given. Therefore whoever is weighed down by the burden of sins, whoever is struck by the darts of temptations, let him confidently flee to the bosom of mother Anne, let him offer prayers and gifts of devotion, and there will be nothing that can prevail against him unto evil. For Anne is called “grace”; according to her name she does not cease to obtain graces for the one who asks, if she has found devout faith. Therefore, faithful of God, celebrate the feasts of the most holy mother; rejoice in her commemoration, and pour out diligent prayers to her, for she is able to free you from every tribulation. Sing joyfully to the Lord our God, all you who love Saint Anne; praise the name of the Lord, all faithful peoples, who love the mother of the God-bearing Virgin. Take Anne for yourselves as patroness, and honor her with devout prayers, and you will always find her a faithful advocate.

By what exercises and devotions we ought to honor the most blessed mother Anne. Chapter 14.

[unclear] We have heard how greatly the most blessed mother Anne avails by her merits before almighty God; we know how worthy she is of honor. It remains now that we briefly say how she is to be honored by us. And although, because of the variety of devotion, a general rule concerning the manner of veneration cannot be set down by us, nevertheless we shall try, as far as we can, to persuade all, so that no one may be able to excuse himself through ignorance from the praise of so great a mother. And indeed, first of all, devotion will establish for each person the manner of praising her; the greater it is, the more useful the manner will be, just as we are accustomed to venerate the other saints with various ceremonies. If perhaps I seem too brief to you, take a fuller manner. Kings, princes, and prelates of churches, if they desire to honor blessed Anne, should erect chapels and oratories in her memory, establish prebends, found monasteries. They should also make diligent prayers to her, celebrate her memory, and feed the poor and needy out of reverence for her. With whatever zeal they venerate the other saints special to themselves, let them know that the holy mother Anne is to be honored not with less but with more abundant zeal. Likewise the prelates of the faithful themselves should have the same manner of veneration, and should institute that the feast of the most holy mother Anne be celebrated by all in their dioceses. They should confer indulgences on the faithful for the cult of Anne, confirm confraternities in her honor, the offerings of prayers in her name

let the abbots also and the other rulers of monks in their monasteries devoutly celebrate the memory of Anne. Let them build chapels and altars. Let them pour forth continual prayers to her. Likewise let the leaders and brothers of the other religious orders do the same as far as they can, and let them never at any time grow lukewarm in the worship of so great a mother. But you, professors of the Carmelite order, who by the title of the most blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary have been specially distinguished with a most ancient privilege, you must venerate and embrace most holy Anne with singular devotion, from whose daughter you have been called venerable. Take care, therefore, that you are never lukewarm in the worship of the mother, you who from her daughter have obtained the name of so great an honor. You also, all the rest, chosen into the lot [unclear], stretch out your souls to the honor of the most holy mother of the Mother of God. Bestow upon her whatever praise you can, and instruct those subject to you, as far as possible, to do the same. You also, O men distinguished by learning in letters, in whom the vein of nocturnal study abounds, dedicate your talents to the blessed mother Anne. Play in verse to her honor, and praise her also in prose as much as you can. But let the simpler, whose talents are slower and not sufficiently suited for composition, copy out with devotion the things that have been published by others; let them read them more often, and for the edification of others also let them affix them to the altars of the holy mother. Let them read prayers suited to her honor. Let them read due praises. Let them read hymns, poems, and proses. Let no one be idle from the praises of Anne; let no one be silent; let no one grow lukewarm. Let all nations redeemed by the blood of Christ celebrate the memory of Anne, from whose merits a great hope of salvation is promised to us. But lest matter for prayer be lacking to the devout worshipers of Anne, three years ago we made, under her honor, a brief prayer in the manner of the angelic salutation, which is now both possessed and read by many. But it seems to us sufficiently fitting that, just as in the rosary of the Mother of God we pay five Lord’s Prayers and fifty angelic salutations, so too we should do to the honor of Saint Anne, yet in such a way that in place of the Ave Maria our prayer which follows is said.

Prayer.

Hail, venerable Anne, mother of the Mother of God, most pleasing to the Holy Trinity, honored above all women. Blessed are you by the Lord, and blessed is the offspring of your womb, [from whom?] the virgin-born Jesus. Amen.

Many appoint this prayer to the honor of Saint Anne in place of the angelic salutation in the rosary, because it is brief and by no means useless. But if our prayer for the rosary of Saint Anne should please anyone, let him read the angelic salutation as is customary, and at the end, after he has said “Jesus Christ,” let him always add this clause: “And blessed be your most honorable mother, Saint Anne, from whom your virginal flesh proceeded without stain. Amen.”

This clause, moreover, the holy Mother of God is said to have revealed to a certain enclosed devotee of hers. If neither this pleases anyone, let him make prayers according to his devotion

another one suited to the honors of the most blessed mother Anne, as best he can. There are also many other pursuits of holy exercise, which are placed in the judgment and devotion of each person. A devout mind will always find a way to honor the most holy Anne with due praises. In fasts and tears, and in alms and prayers, in acts of penance and disciplines, in song and readings, the most blessed mother is to be honored by us. But it is no small offense that we find no fitting history concerning the holy mother Anne which is in every respect suitable to her honor and feast. For the history now in use in many places, in diverse forms, is varied and not, as it seems to many, sufficiently elegant, since it is less worthy of such merits and in very many places seems apocryphal. Nor is there only one, but several are found, as seemed good to each person, with additions that are less approved. What shall I say about the office of the Mass, which we see is confused in many places by a similar variety? An office is sung by very many which a certain devout person, changing the meanings of the words but retaining the melody, drew from the Saturday office of blessed Mary; this seems less useful for devotion, since hearers, deceived by the similarity of the melody, think that the celebration is not about Saint Anne but about the Mother of God. If the subject is acceptable, at least let the melody be changed. Yet all these things could easily be corrected, if the authority of some pontiff intervened; relying on it, learned men in these matters could compose a history and an office regulated in sense and melody and approved by the Scriptures.

That the most blessed mother Anne rewards her worshippers in manifold ways both in this life and in the life to come. Chapter 14

If the frequent display of miracles wins reverence for the saints, blessed Anne is most worthy of the highest honor, for she daily bestows so many and such great benefits upon those who worship her according to their vows that there is no one who could recount them all. Indeed we know many miracles of Saint Anne, both new and ancient; but it is not our intention now to turn our mind to these, which we have learned are called into doubt by many, not because they contain any falsehood in themselves, but because most modern men, who seem learned to themselves, do not believe miracles but disparage them. Therefore we do not wish to give occasion for disparagement, nor to expose the present treatise to suspicion, lest they say that we write not correct things but apocryphal ones. For no one understands, no one believes, no one grasps how many benefits God daily confers on the lovers of Saint Anne, unless devout experience instructs him. But we know that through the invocation of Saint Anne many powerful, learned, noble, and ignoble men, virgins and women, young and old, have often been freed from the greatest tribulations, snatched from dangers, and miraculously helped in necessities. Many religious persons also of both sexes

and laypersons, by the merits of Anne, we have found very often to have been freed from the gravest temptations of flesh and spirit; others, placed in want and poverty, to have been unexpectedly and abundantly provided for through Anne’s suffrages; others to have been cured from a grave calamity. Who could enumerate how many have been healed from the ruinous sadness of mind and melancholy by the aid of the most pious mother Anne? How many also, secure amid adversities, fearless among enemies and robbers, safe amid the perils of the sea, have escaped? Anne, most holy mother, has been accustomed to rescue many devoted to her from various temptations, to free them from the contagion of pestilence, and to cure them from various illnesses. Who can recount how many she has brought back from the worst despair to hope of mercy; how many she has recalled from the hardest habit of sin to the paths of penitence; how many living lukewarmly in religion and outside it she has inflamed with the fire of divine love? By her merits and suffrages women in childbirth have been freed from dangers otherwise close to death. Many also, as we read, have been snatched from the sentence of perpetual damnation. Finally, it is said that she has guarded some of her devotees from the disgrace of infamy; it is recorded that she has freed others from desperate sickness, some from chains and prisons, and certain ones even from the imminent dangers of death. We read also that by her merits some have been called back from death to life; others, at the point of death, have been most mercifully visited by her and, before they left the world, made already secure concerning heaven. Often too she is said to have enlightened the dull wits of certain persons, so that those who before had been despised as without learning afterwards became objects of admiration to many. She is said at times to have strengthened orators when invoked, so that they not only found themselves constant but also made readier in speaking. Things lost, therefore, we read, have finally been wonderfully found through the invocation of Anne. But why do I strive into immensity? For if I had a voice of iron and a hundred tongues, I could not run through all Anne’s benefits by which she is accustomed to come to the aid of her devotees. Indeed, as many benefits of hers are found as there are inconveniences of human life. From whatever tribulation anyone cries to her with devotion, he is able to obtain help. She extinguishes the flames of carnal concupiscence. She turns the ruinous sadness of mind into saving joy. She gives the necessities of life. She preserves a good and fair reputation. She frees women who are in peril in childbirth. She lessens pains. She puts demons to flight. Invoked, she comes to the aid of those laboring in tribulation; she brings travelers back to their own country; she hears the wretched who cry to her. She knows how to give all things which it is lawful for a Christian person to ask, provided that devoted faith commends the one who prays. But concerning all the things which we have touched upon only briefly in commemorating them generally, we have at hand particular examples that have actually occurred, by which we could recount not uncertain things in writing, but deeds in truth. Yet it is not our purpose to compose a history, but

to declare the praises of our Lady, divine Anne, with as much simplicity as we can. Nor indeed would I have said that she is to be venerated because of miracles, but because of piety toward God. So many and so great miracles concerning the blessed mother Anne have become known to me that, if I wished to write them all, I would be forced to enlarge this treatise excessively. The greatest of all miracles is if, by her merits, we may deserve to receive compunction and forgiveness of our sins; if we may overcome evil habit; if we may arrive at eternal life. For this end, and no other, she is to be venerated by us.

Chapter XV.

Because in these last days, as the charity of many grows cold, iniquity abounds, it is very necessary for us, my brothers, that just as we fall almost daily by sinning, so also through frequent zeal for holy exercise we may be renewed every day in good will. For there was never any institution so holy among human customs that with time it did not grow lukewarm from its first fervor. Thus all the orders of religious life, failing with the passage of time, have departed from their first institution; and unless by the diligence of the elders they had often been reformed to the regular paths of life, they would always have remained in their deformity. Among Christians too something similar is happening, for today they are found to have fallen far away from the first institution of the faith. Where now is the former fervor of our faith? Where the devotion of the people? Where the holy conduct of priests? Charity has grown cold, and all zeal for religion, together with it, has for the most part perished from human beings. Who would believe how great a loss the evil morals of Christians have brought about? Behold, as God permits it because of the crimes of human beings, the unbelieving Saracens, Turks, Tartars, and the other enemies of the Catholic faith, after slaughtering Christians, have brought Asia, Africa, the Hellespont, and a great part of Europe under their power, so that the twentieth part of the world which once was Christian is not Christian today. And in truth, unless the compassion of almighty God preserves the remnants left in Europe, in a short time an end will have been made of the Christian name. Since, therefore, weighed down by our sins, we are not able to obtain God’s mercy, the suffrages of the saints must be implored by us with diligent prayers, so that, appeased by their merits, the eternal Judge may grant us pardon and peace, which we do not deserve. And lest devotion fail over time, as is its custom, it must be labored over with great care, so that through the mutual exhortation of the brothers perseverance may follow. Hence a praiseworthy custom has grown strong in the Church of God: that the faithful establish congregations in honor of certain saints, which, for the increase of devotion, they call fraternities. Thus knights act in honor of Saint George, archers in honor of Sebastian the martyr, pilgrims in honor of James the apostle from Galicia

Now therefore, if we believe these and similar confraternities of the saints to be useful for obtaining God’s mercy for the people, we trust that those which are established in memory of the most blessed Mother of God and of Anne, her most holy mother, are better. For by as much as the Mother of God, together with her venerable mother, surpasses the other saints in heaven in merits and holiness, by so much does a confraternity dedicated to her name hold a more eminent place. Hence the faithful, moved by pious devotion, in order that they might deserve to have her as a ready advocate with God, established in her honor a confraternity under the name of the Rosary, which has now become so widespread through various regions of the world that there is scarcely any province in which several are not found.

But the devout worshippers of the most blessed Anne, considering that from these confraternities the devotion of the faithful could greatly profit, thought to erect, after the example of the Rosary, a praiseworthy congregation in honor of the holy mother Anne, so that the name and praises of so great a patroness might be able to come to the knowledge of many. And so this holy confraternity began in the diocese of Osnaburg, and, having been confirmed by Conrad, bishop of the said church, almost a decade before this under Frederick III, it was greatly multiplied. Then Rumuldus de Laupach, prior of the convent of the Carmelites at Frankfurt, a very great worshipper and lover of the holy mother Anne, at the urging of certain nobles established the same confraternity in his aforesaid convent; Berthold of Henneberg, most reverend archbishop of the church of Mainz, confirmed it, and the supreme pontiff Innocent VIII, in the eighth year of his pontificate, approved the same by apostolic authority. And indeed it is a worthy institution, that the Carmelite friars, who are especially distinguished by the title of the most blessed Mother of God, should also be more ready in the praises of her mother.

Today there is a great and abundant number of persons of both sexes in this confraternity, who daily do and expend wonderful and many things for the honor of Saint Anne. Moreover, in various places this same venerable confraternity is erected by the faithful and celebrated with fitting devotion. Yet detractors of every good thing are found, as from the beginning, also of this honorable confraternity, who tear it with impious tooth and assail it with ruinous presumption. What displeases you in this most holy confraternity, O profane detractors? What will you have against it? Bring it forth, that we may hear. You say: These confraternities are superstitious, because they render the Catholic faith weak, withdraw due worship from God, and despise obedience to the parish churches. These are the heads of the opposing party, the crimes of an unjust accusation, the charges of wicked detraction. To these we shall briefly respond in order.

This fraternity of the most blessed mother Anne is not superstitious, as you say, O impious slanderers, but is true, upright, holy, in which the worship of God is not diminished but increased; obedience is not despised but commended; even the catholic faith is not weakened by this holy fraternity, as you think, but renewed and defended, while through the exercises of holy charity it is illumined, that it may be formed. But as for your lament that the parish churches are deserted, that must be imputed in no small measure to your own offenses: you demand milk and wool from the sheep of the Lord, yet you do not feed the sheep themselves as first of all you ought to have done, nor do you guard them. Why do you pretend that offerings are being denied to you, when you abound in many riches? The Lord Christ is shepherd of shepherds and vicar. If he wished the faithful to be free in hearing masses, there is no one who can prevent him. You have not seen all the privileges of monks, nor will you see them. Who does not know that for your purses you wage war against holy fraternities, and that you tear at monks not from love of God, but of gold? Behold, the supreme pontiff has confirmed this fraternity; behold, Berthold, archbishop of Mainz, than whom there is no other more excellent, approved it by ordinary authority, and you foolish men still murmur. Cease, I beseech you, cease from this folly, and do not censure what you know such great pontiffs to have approved. Believe me, it is not good to stretch out the tongue against the saints of God; it is not good to wish to prohibit the devotion of so many people toward Saint Anne. He draws very near to confusion who opens his mouth against Saint Anne. If you do not believe my words, observe those who are such, and by experience you will know that I have spoken the truth. It is rash to censure a good which is seen to come to many for salvation. Many benefits come to devout people from the celebration of this most happy fraternity; those who are strangers to it are for the most part without them. It also draws its worshippers to charity toward God and neighbor, creates the concord of brotherly love, calls them back from vices and sins, and inflames desire for the love of heavenly happiness. I pass over how many masses, how many prayers, how many alms, how many sacred works are done daily in this fraternity, which otherwise would be entirely omitted. Would that the Almighty might illumine the hearts of all Christians toward similar exercises of devotion; would that he might inflame the minds of all to duly honor this fraternity. How much devotion, how much peace, and how much concord could abound in the catholic Church! Indeed, if all were to come together in this fraternity, it could happen that, through love of the holy mother Anne, they would cease from mutual injuries and be made more eager in the observance of God’s commandments. For true fraternity cultivates and nourishes brotherly love, nor does devotion allow those to be unlike whom the observance of so great a congregation has made concordant in love of most holy Anne. O who will grant that this holy fraternity, spread throughout the whole Christian world, may be celebrated, so that all the faithful in

may be carried away into love of Saint Anne, and, while they anticipate one another in holy unity, may cease from wars and mutual insults out of reverence for so great a patroness. It is a fraternity plainly useful and always to be honored, which gives form to faith by works, raises up hope, stirs charity, and kindles devotion. For through it sluggishness is shaken from the minds of the faithful, and the fervor of holy renewal is inspired. He who attacks it is mad; he who speaks against it is more deranged than a deranged man; he who strives to destroy it begrudges Christian salvation. Many things indeed still ought to have been said in praise of this most holy fraternity, had not the occupation of household affairs claimed me for itself. But what has been said by me against its adversaries was uttered not with the intention of railing at them, but of correcting and amending them. Yet I trust that there are few who set themselves against the holy mother and her fraternity.

Conclusion of this work and apology. Chapter 16.

On the insufficiency of the author, with an exhortation of the fraternity.

Although from the beginning I had proposed to write more concerning the praises of the most holy mother Anne, nevertheless from this point it has now pleased me to stop, lest, if I extended the treatise without measure, I should smother the reader’s devotion by excessive length. For those who desire to persuade others must be found brief in speech and abundant in the majesty of their thoughts. From the first point I do not at all trust that I have gone astray; but what I have accomplished in the second will be judged by those who are going to read this labor of mine, such as it is. I have satisfied my promise; I have also satisfied my friends; but neither my devotion nor the dignity of the subject has been satisfied. I wished more than I could do, and I did less than I wished. Finally, who is sufficient to venerate with worthy praises Anne, the parent of the most blessed mother of God? I confess, therefore, that I am unworthy to speak of the most holy mother, since I am a sinful man and wrapped in offenses from my youth. Yet I could not keep silent from her praise, because necessity lay upon me, and devotion, strongly fortified by the prayers of friends, pressed me on. But after I had come thus far, the excellence of the subject overcame my impatient heat of summer, so that henceforth I ought to honor in silence her whom I am not sufficient to praise. Whatever, however, has been said and written by me in this work, I submit to the holy Roman Church and to all learned Catholic men, from whose definitive judgment I never intend to dissent. Whatever the most holy Roman Church determines is to be believed will be for me the firmest faith. Finally we turn our speech to you, friends, worshipers, brothers and sisters of the most holy mother Anne, asking that you receive in good part what has been written by us out of great devotion to the praise of so great a mother, and that with devout prayers you knock at the door of the holy patroness, so that with her accustomed loving-kindness she may come to our aid, take away our faults, obtain virtues for us, and secure eternal life. We also exhort you to take care to persevere in the love and fraternity of the most holy mother, honoring her with continual praises, so that, absolved from faults by her merits, you may lead a tranquil life here and an eternal life after this life.

Here ends the book of lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict, On the Praises of Saint Anne.

There follows a tetrastich on the most holy mother Anne.

Tetrastich of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, on the most holy mother Anne.

Venerable Anne, mother of the life-giving Virgin, Excellent in merits and mighty in loving-kindness: No one goes away sad who worships and venerates you; For you bring to all the gentle aid of salvation.

Distich of the same, which he placed by the image of Saint Anne.

Whoever in adversities has appealed to Saint Anne With devout prayers, he will be well protected.

Tetrastich of Conrad Celtis Protucius, poet laureate, on Saint Anne.

Anne has never dismissed anyone’s prayers empty, But, radiant, has always brought the desired aid. Therefore let us heap great honor upon the pious mother, Who allows no one’s prayers to be empty.

Tetrastich of Theodoricus Gresmundus the Younger of Mainz to Saint Anne.

Hail, Anne, parent of the Virgin Mary, Auspicious, worthy to begin the work of our salvation. Since human redemption was begun through you, I pray, Continue it by your prayers, covering our crimes.

Distich by Rudolf Langius, canon of Munster, on Saint Anne.

Great parent Anne, mother of the fruitful Virgin, hear the vows which pregnant women bring to you.

Tetrastich by Jodocus Badius of Ghent, on Saint Anne.

Anne, ornament of the world, mother of the mother of Jesus, may your grandson, for the merits of your daughter, give us the stars. Holy Anne, parent of the first fruits of our salvation, help us with your offspring and with your grandson.

Rudolf Agricola, in his poem on Saint Anne, among other things, says:

Anne, parent of the highest parent, venerable mother, you who first open to peoples the way of salvation: from you all diseases flee, and pallor and pain, and all harmful things that settle in the mind and in the body. Whatever it is among men that wearies cares and hearts flees from you, as clouds driven away are wont to flee the winds.

Rutgerus Venrai, canon regular of Hainaut, to the image of Saint Anne.

Here pour forth devout prayers, knee bent, where Anne the parent sits blessed with her offspring. Do not doubt that you will obtain whatever you ask of her, for powerful Anne continually shines through her prayers.

Distich by the same on Saint Anne.

Hail, Anne, parent of the mother of Jesus Christ; we ask you, drive every wickedness away from us.

Rosary of Saint Anne by Jodocus Beisselius, patrician of Aachen, to the reverend father lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict.

Whoever shall wish to read this rosary for devotion in honor of the most blessed mother should begin with the Lord's Prayer together with the salutation of Saint Anne, which he should always repeat after two verses; this salutation is as follows.

Hail, venerable Anne, mother of the mother of God, most pleasing to the Holy Trinity, honored before all women. Blessed are you by the Lord, and blessed is the offspring of your womb, and Jesus Christ, born of the virginity of your offspring. Amen. Our Father. Hail, mother of God.

Anne, may it be permitted to wretched me to utter your praises; for, if you allow it, I shall bring you garlands and roses. Hail.

Anne, you shine, venerable offspring of the kings of Judah, and also renowned through Joachim, your pious husband. Hail.

Anne, long barren, you wept in the love of your husband, the one glory and one honor of married women. But let her, by holy posterity, worship God. Hail.

Pious Anne, you seek offspring, and not for vain uses; 'Rejoice,' he says, 'behold, as a mother you shall have offspring, exulting.' Hail.

Anne, you shall bear offspring blessed with such great virtue that she shall shine with virginal honor as mother. Hail.

Anne, you shall bear pleasing offspring whom the world does not contain; God himself willingly enters her chaste womb. Hail.

Anne, from your blood at last shall arise blood which, when poured out, shall bring hope continually to wretched sinners. Hail.

Anne, so great an expectation befitted your birth-giving; it is no easy thing to be regarded as the mother of the mother of God. Hail.

All ages too shall proclaim you blessed. Our Father. Hail, mother of God.

Anne, you conceived Mary pure from evil, it is believed, and soon had her holy for God. Hail.

Anne, in your womb you bear her whom figures marked out, whom the holy fathers foretold as to come. Hail.

Anne, you bear the enclosed paradise, the tree of life, blessed and sacred with all the honor of the field. Hail.

Anne, heavy with child, you bear the garden which the flaming sword of the cherubim guards, glowing night and day. Hail.

Anne, you bear the flower that surpasses white lilies, and [unclear]. Hail.

Anne, you bear the bride of the true Solomon, and a house adorned inside and out with every gem. Hail.

Anne, you bear the temple whose inner chambers

The sounds have filled [the air], music and every rejoicing: Hail. Anne, you bear the veil, fair beneath the image of the fathers: Hail. Holding within itself the deeds, because it may cover the lofty things of God: Hail. Anne, you bear the offspring whose head the golden flame of Phoebus clothes: Hail. And the bright moon clothes her snowy feet: Hail. Our Father. Hail of God.

Anne, now made possessor of the longed-for Mary: Hail. You scarcely contain in your whole breast the joys that have arisen: Hail. Anne, all things applauded the newly born Mary: Hail. The stars, and an unwonted radiance flowed from the pole: Hail. Anne, it is right to believe that angelic choirs celebrated around you: Hail. The birthday of your offspring: Hail. Anne, the shades of the deep felt your childbirth: Hail. Then that new light terrified the Stygian pools: Hail. Anne, as mother you hesitate to touch your daughter with your hands: Hail. More ruddy than the sun and than the lights of heaven: Hail. Anne, why do you fear to handle the heavenly girl? Hail. She smiles at her mother; she causes no sadness: Hail. Anne, take courage; behold, the daughter reaches toward your milky breasts: Hail. And seeks with tender hands your neck: Hail. Anne, you break off delays, baring breasts and bosom: Hail. You receive her tender little limbs in your tender lap: Hail. Anne, you cherish your daughter, and from your breast she draws sweet juices: Hail. With her rosy mouth, making pleasing murmurs: Hail. Anne, if you knew how many sufferings your daughter will bear: Hail. And how many deaths she will bear, you would now be nothing: Hail. Our Father. Hail of God.

Anne, it is your concern to adorn your daughter with approved: Hail. Manners, and to make her fit for the highest God: Hail. Anne, you prepare to bring your daughter into the lofty temple: Hail. But of her own accord the kindly one reached the step of those above: Hail. Anne, you follow the swift one with slow pace and toil: Hail. The ready little virgin consoles her weary mother: Hail. Anne, why do you wonder at strength in the tender virgin? Hail. You see not human things, but the holy signs of God: Hail. Anne, you are accustomed to give gifts to the needy and to sacred temples: Hail. Now you give that than which no woman ever gave more: Hail. Anne, when you wished your consecrated daughter to live: Hail. You gladly entered the cloister, and the virginal house: Hail. Anne, about to send away the pious one, you [unclear] cheeks and eyes with weeping: Hail. Deep love holds you unmoved: Hail. Anne, return home; send your daughter to the Thunderer: Hail. Let her think of nothing except the Jesus who is to come: Hail. Anne, let your daughter fly through the ethereal recesses: Hail. Let love sent from the highest summit possess her: Hail. Anne, it is enough for you to serve two Marys: Hail. They also will honor me, not with small devotion, and you: Hail. Our Father. Hail of God.

Anne, by your own weeping you have been taught to succor one who weeps: Hail. Hence you too readily favor the wretched man with his vows: Hail. Anne, you are accustomed to overturn the fixed laws of nature: Hail. And thus you will desire it: let the barren woman now be a joyful mother: Hail. Anne, you also halt the gifts of fleeting fortune: Hail. Lest, slipping suddenly, they flee from our bosoms: Hail. You relieve mourning, and love yields to you: Hail. Anne, you help whether hostile force terrifies someone, or whether: Hail. The savage chains of a dark prison hold him: Hail. Anne, be present as relief for sick mortals: Hail. With you as guide, lost life returns to the languishing: Hail. Anne, you provide things always to be feared for the timid tyrant: Hail. If the winds and wave toss a battered ship: Hail. Anne, mortal hearts cannot ask from you in vain: Hail. And whatever you will, your daughter and God will will: Hail. Anne, therefore blessed in merits and in so great an offspring: Hail. Anne, great mother, look upon our prayers: Hail.

Prayer to be said after the rosary

Almighty and most merciful God, who deigned to choose blessed Anne as the mother of the mother of your Son, graciously grant that we, who honor her memory with faithful devotion, may through her merits and prayers obtain the helps of eternal life. Through the same.

Here ends the rosary of Jodocus Beissel, professor of both laws, patrician of Aachen, addressed to the reverend father and lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, of the order of Saint Benedict. From Aachen, on the third day before the Ides of April, in the year 1493.

Poem of Adewernherus of Themar on most holy Anne, to the Reverend Father and Lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot

In praise of the renowned grandmother we sing; Jesus, dear grandson, move the plectra of the heart, and you, the daughter, chaste mother, do not be absent from the choir as it sings.

Anne, offspring of kings, long remains childless with her husband; she laments herself barren; weeping, she prays for offspring, and her tears do not flow in vain.

Heavenly messengers promise offspring; pregnant, joined to her husband, then in childbirth, she is proved a mother by the child through whom our salvation came.

Thus the venerable stock of Jesse grew green; a fruitful rod comes forth with fertile shoot, by whose flower, made perfect, we live again through death.

By this birth Joachim is made worthy to stand in the shrines, removing the pontiff’s reproaches. Thus, Anne, prepare us to bring pure prayers to your grandson.

Commend us to the boy whom your pious chastity bore as a mother; by prayer we ask this. O blessed matron, Christ denies you nothing.

To Christ, who is consort with the Father and the Spirit, who reigns, be glory through all ages, whom they give as reconciled. Amen.

This hymn, however, is sung to the tune of that one which, on the Nativity of Saint Mary, is used by many churches, and begins “Rejoice in your inmost bowels, mother,” etc. From Heidelberg Castle, the third kalends of February, 1493.

Poem or hymn of Johannes [Herbsluterburgensis?] on Saint Anne, to the Reverend Father and Lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot

Rejoice, Anne, refuge for the wretched; we pray, we sing, we bring forth praises now to you on the feast; be gracious with your offspring.

Rejoice, earth shining, fertile with grass, and wet with abundant deifying dew, from which was born the Virgin, purer than ether, knowing no sin.

Rejoice, you who were of royal seed; now, conceived, given to a husband, you had led long in marriage without offspring; a mother in childbed, your vows were fulfilled.

Rejoice, you who blushed at the pontiff’s reproach and were confounded; you call upon God with tears. Heard, you receive your husband as he comes to meet you at the gate called Golden.

Rejoice, you who, joyful, embraced Joachim your husband as he met you, taught by deity, and thus the mother of heaven, and of your Jesus, is conceived in the womb.

Rejoice, simple wisdom, discerning with angelic insight, which praises in choir, and, divided threefold, you distribute your goods to the temple and to the poor, and a part to your servants.

Rejoice: the people of the faithful celebrates your feasts, as their patroness; and with the Father, the Spirit, and Christ the Son, by your petitions, Anne, may you render them propitious. Amen.

This hymn takes the melody of that which is sung concerning the Ascension of the Lord, namely “Now the solemn feast,” etc., and that one concerning martyrs, “Renowned by the merit of the saints,” etc. From Heidelberg, [unclear] nones of February, in the year 1493.

Elegiac poem of Rutger Venray, canon regular in Haina, of the diocese of Worms, on Saint Anne

Hail, bright mother of the Virgin Mother, of the Father’s splendor, of the brightness of untouched light. You bore for the Lord the divine, holy maiden, from whom Jesus, kindly light of the world, came forth.

Speak steadfastly to your grandson the groaning of your daughter, although he himself made the heavens and the ground. Your grandson in the flesh, Jesus himself, joined supreme deity to flesh, for he is God and man.

Therefore, although Jesus has always existed, nevertheless he chooses and deigns to be called your grandson. Do not hesitate to strike such a grandson with prayers. Anne, we ask you, and you will bear all things asked.

If he has not bent ready ears at the first petitions, Anne, return more quickly to your daughter. Let your daughter show her breasts to her son Christ; straightway the kindly mother will obtain what is desired.

If the matter is very difficult to obtain by prayer, let the daughter seek aid together with her mother. My faith is firm, and I do not doubt that straightway the Lord will hear both as they pray with gracious ear.

Therefore, brothers, with continual prayers one must seek the aid of Anne and of Mary alike. It is certain that, if you honor the mother of the mother of the Lord, you yourself worship her under the title of mother of the Virgin.

Again, if you venerate the mother of the Lord, it becomes clear what praises you prepare for the Lord in his mother. To the daughter, to the son, be praise, power, and honor of Anne, and to the highest Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

Sapphic poem of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, on the day of Saint Anne

Let us celebrate the sacred feasts of Anne, of the exalted mother, rich in merits, who brought forth into the world the parent of God the Father’s Son.

Her life, always to be venerated by us, is deservedly praised as blessed; by the gift of signs she increases relief for wretched minds.

She heals the languid, purges all evils, brightens the hearts of the sorrowful with rejoicing, orders what is fitting, rules and governs, smooths rough things.

Mighty, sitting in the court of the highest King, she will wipe away stains and sins; she bestows grace, faithful souls

She leads into heaven. Here the brothers who frequent your feasts, utering their vows, praying good things to you: help, preserve, cherish, govern, renowned mother.

May honor and power be to the high Thunderer, who, God simple and likewise threefold, has bestowed on Anne the crown of great glory forever. Amen.

This Sapphic hymn is sung to the melody of “Ut queant laxis,” “Vita sanctorum,” “Virginis proles,” “Quo chorus vatum,” “Iste confessor,” and similar hymns, which are Sapphic only. From Sponheim, on the Nones of July, in the year of the Lord 1494.

An elegiac poem by Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, concerning the holy mother Anne.

How great the rewards Anne gives back to those who worship her, no one grasps in mind nor can speak with the mouth. She drives away hardships, obtains pardon, increases ornaments of honor for her own, and makes them be in heaven. Too many bitter things, by contrast, accompany those who despise mother Anne; look out for yourself, wicked one. She crushes the proud, casts the powerful down from honor, and allows them often to suffer great scandals. This is plain and remains fixed: Anne offers joyful things to those who honor her, but brings many sorrows to her enemies. Therefore, men, I advise you: serve so great a patroness; and let the choir of women also be present together in love. It is also clearly established by examples that she helps pious hearts. From Sponheim, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, 1493.

A Sapphic poem by Rutgerus Siccamber, as a hymn in praise of Saint Anne.

We sing your praises, venerable Anne; favor the melodies of those who praise you, obtaining pardon for all, and giving the rewards of salvation.

You, Anne, parent of Christ’s mother, dwelling in the highest citadel of heaven, obtain whatever you seek from the begotten son of the Almighty.

You heal the sick, cleanse what is stained, make your faithful servants attain their vow, and finally make them climb to the heavenly kingdom in the threefold realm.

By your approved conduct, Anne, you bent the highest Lord, and by many prayers, that he should grant you to become in the world parent of so great an offspring.

To the highest Father, to the heavenly Son, to the sacred Spirit be honor and power, brightness, virtue, piety, and vigor through all ages.

Another by the same.

Let us all resound the diligent praises of Anne, mother of the Virgin Mother, with all our strength, from the marrow of the soul, with ringing voice.

She brought forth for our wretched race, stained with the defilement of mother Eve, a noble offspring, and gave to the world a radiant beam.

This light of the world drove away the shadows of the darkened world, radiating all with heavenly light, as holy John proclaims in the sacred book.

Anne, mother of the divine girl, whose begotten son you call your grandson in the flesh only, do not disdain the people praying to you.

Virgin, favor the earnest prayers of your mother Anne, who asks for us. You, grandson Jesus, readily fulfill her prayer.

To the Son of Anne’s daughter and mother, with God most high, be honor and power; equal honor to the blessed Spirit for all time.

Another iambic dimeter poem by the same, which is sung to the melody of Ambrose’s hymns.

Let us, bowed down, honor Anne’s blessed feast, singing due thanks with our voices and from our inmost hearts.

She is the mother of the kindly Virgin, who brought forth the radiance of the world; she is the one who, by virtues, made herself most pleasing to God.

She repels harms and grants grace by her prayers; she relieves grievous diseases, of the body as well as of the spirit.

In praise of [unclear], king of heaven, to you with ringing songs, and at the same time to the Son and the Spirit, we utter pious praises. Amen.

An Alcmanian poem by the same, which is sung to the melody “Crux fidelis” or “Pange lingua.”

This company, with voice and vows and pious hearts, is eager, mother Anne, to proclaim your feasts so splendidly.

Be present kindly, we pray, to those who praise you together. You are the parent of Mary’s mother; you are most pleasing to God.

You preserved the beginnings of the Law which Moses once bestowed on the ancient fathers and on the Hebrew peoples.

You obtain wondrous, gracious gifts for the faithful by pleasing intercession with the Son of the high Father.

You heal the sick, and grant that hearts be chaste.

We beseech you, Father, and the Son with the Spirit, that you grant joys to us who hold the renowned praises of sweetest Anne, the kindly mother of the Virgin. Amen.

Poem of Rutger, a venerable German regular canon of Heyn[?], on the book On the Praises of Saint Anne

Whoever you shall be, reader of this excellent book, put aside empty fear: it contains no trifles. Abbot Trithemius, by his art, has published this book, pregnant with wondrous meaning and sweet with charm: he who watches over books, guardian of the Sponheim flock, who cultivates the sacred writings of the threefold tongue. Here you will find titles of Anne full of reason and art; only turn them over in a pious heart. He does not follow vain and everywhere doubtful little tales; he teaches the clear streams of sacred eloquence. Therefore, I pray, read the worthy praises of venerable Anne, which the learned man presents to you, beloved one.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, sends greeting to the reader. Since recently, at the urging of friends, I had resolved to write something on the praises of the most holy mother Anne, certain fathers of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel asked that I not omit the defense of the most pure conception of Mary. And so, moved by their prayers and otherwise by just reasoning, I designated the seventh chapter of this work for the conception of the Mother of God and Virgin. Lest anyone take it in a sense other than mine, I thought the reader should be warned. For I know, and it has not escaped me, that many most holy and most learned men once wrote that the Mother of God was subject to the stain of original sin, men who flourished long before the Council of Basel. Granting this opinion to its own time, I pass over it wholly untouched, and I do not intend to say or write anything at all against them. But indeed, if anything is seen to have been said by me rather harshly, let it be referred not to those who thought otherwise than we do, but only to the obstinate, who, prattling without learning, do not shrink from calling the defenders of the other opinion heretics. And my words show this, because they indicate the present time and not the past. For when I say, “Why do fools bark? Why do the inexperienced murmur?” it belongs to the present time, not to the past; and today the obstinate are reproved, not those in former times who thought otherwise. But when you ask who ever wrote the contrary, I do not bring charges against the ancient fathers, but I mean those who, after the determination of the aforesaid council, hold another opinion. And so I reproach only the obstinacy of certain unlearned men of this time, not the opinion of learned men, whoever they may be, who think otherwise, especially since I am not ignorant of the declaration of the supreme pontiff Sixtus IV. It has seemed to me, however, by no means alien from the holy Roman Church to venerate the faith of the most pure conception, which she believes and venerates, as is shown today by many documents. Finally, with the doctors of the universities of Paris, Cologne, Heidelberg, Erfurt, Vienna, Leipzig, Tübingen, Ingolstadt, Basel, Mainz, and many others, and with nearly all the orders and the faithful of Christ spread throughout the whole Christian world, I do not fear to venerate the conception of the Mother of God and Virgin Mary as pure. Yet I do not admit obstinacy, but I wish to obey the Roman Church in all things as the most reverend mother of all churches. This is the pure and sincere meaning of my aforesaid chapter, in which I think no one who holds an opinion soberly and without obstinacy is disparaged. Farewell, reader.

This letter of the aforesaid lord Johannes the abbot is missing from certain copies through carelessness and negligence; yet he himself ordered it to be appended to all copies, and decreed that it be regarded as appended to each one.
